blocks.text: I looked at the photograph for a long time. A small boy, maybe six, in a Spurs T-shirt, holding a toy airplane. And then I remembered.

It was the end of my shift, July 1998. I was pushing my cart toward the service elevator when I saw a man in a baseball cap leading a little boy by the wrist toward the loading dock. The boy was crying and saying, in Spanish, "I want my papi." The man answered in English, sharply. Something was wrong. I stepped in front of them and told the boy, in Spanish, that I was his tia and he should come with me for a cookie. The man tried to pull him away. I started shouting for security. He let go and ran out the loading dock door.
I took the boy into the linen room, gave him a cookie from my lunch bag, and sang to him while I waited for security.
They came and took him to the front desk. A manager told me to go home and not to talk about it. I was young, I didn't have my papers yet, and I was afraid of losing my job. So I didn't.
I never knew what happened next. I never knew it wasn't over.

The incident report filled in what I'd missed. The man in the baseball cap had been hired by the boy's grandfather, a wealthy rancher in a bitter custody fight with his son, the boy's father. When the first attempt failed because of me, the grandfather's people paid off the hotel's head of security to erase the tapes and write the incident up as a "lost child, found." Two days later, they tried again at a different hotel, and succeeded. The boy, Lucas, was taken to Mexico.
His father spent four years searching before he got him back through the courts.

But I'd seen the man's face. And before I went home that night, I'd scribbled the license plate of the truck that sped away from the loading dock on a hotel notepad and slipped it under the door of the guest in Room 614, the boy's father. I'd forgotten that too. The father had kept that slip of paper. It was the lead that eventually found his son.

Lucas is thirty-four now, an engineer in Houston. His father, Javier, is seventy. Javier had spent years trying to find the housekeeper who wrote that plate number, but the hotel's records listed only "staff member, name unknown." Then last month, during renovations, a new manager found the original, unaltered incident report in a storage box, with my name on it.
The general manager, after making a phone call to the hotel's owners, told me I could keep the check.

Javier and Lucas came back to the hotel the following week. Lucas brought me a toy airplane, the same kind he'd been holding in that photograph. He said he didn't remember my face, but he remembered someone singing to him in a room full of towels.
I used the money to pay off my house and help my granddaughter with college. I kept working, though. Somebody has to watch the elevators.
